newsitem.title: GERMANY: German tax revenues short of target - magazine.
newsitem.headline: German tax revenues short of target - magazine.

text.p: German tax revenues are falling short of target, despite a big downward revision in estimates last May, news weekly Focus said on Saturday.

The magazine, in a report released ahead of its Monday edition, said that budget experts from Chancellor Helmut Kohl's conservative coalition expected revenue forecasts in October to show a shortfall of between two and three billion marks.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel, seeking to complete the passage of a 70 billion mark ($45.94 billion) savings package for next year, has said he would review the results of the tax estimates before deciding whether further budget cuts are needed next year.

Waigel has committed Germany to fulfilling the terms of the Maastricht treaty on qualifying for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU). He has targeted a budget deficit of 2.5 percent of gross domestic for 1997, against a Maastricht limit of at or near three percent of GDP.

Revenue estimates were revised down by 20 billion marks in May after a hard winter caused the economy to shrink in the first quarter. Focus said that value-added tax was the main culprit for the new shortfall, although corporation tax was running above expectations.

A finance ministry spokesman declined to comment on the tax estimates, which will be reviewed by a working group of federal and regional officials only at the beginning of November. Until then, no concrete figures are expected, the spokesman added.
